summary.title: Chapter 6 - Monitoring Distributed Systems
summary.one_liner: Google SRE's principles for deciding what should page a human, how to choose metrics (the four golden signals), and how to keep monitoring simple and low-noise.
takeaways: Page a human only for urgent, actionable, user-visible problems; avoid alerting on something that merely seems weird.
Monitor the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) and distinguish successful from failed request latency.
Prefer symptom-based alerts over cause-based alerts, and use white-box monitoring for debugging and imminent problems.
Measure tail latency with histograms and percentiles rather than means, which can hide slow requests.
Keep alerting rules simple and robust; remove rarely used or unused signals to limit complexity.
summary.summary: This chapter from Google's SRE book sets out principles for monitoring and alerting: defining terms like monitoring, alerts, pages, and root cause, and explaining why each page costs human time and attention. It contrasts symptom-oriented black-box monitoring with cause-oriented white-box monitoring and introduces the four golden signals as a minimum set of user-facing metrics. It also covers measurement resolution, tail latency via histograms, and a checklist of questions for evaluating whether an alert is worth paging. Two case studies (Bigtable over-alerting and Gmail's scriptable responses) illustrate the trade-offs in practice.
